newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistani foreign minister visits Washington.
newsitem.headline: Pakistani foreign minister visits Washington.

text.p: Pakistan's Foreign Minister Gohar Ayub Khan, making his first visit to Washington since Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif's government took power in February, said he wanted to cement relations with the United States.

"The objective is to bring about better understanding of the Nawaz Sharif government, the Pakistan government, with the United States," Khan said before leaving on Sunday for his three-day visit to the U.S.

"We always have very good relations...We want to further cement our relations and improve those relations so that we can play a more effective role -- both Pakistan and the United States -- in the region we are in," he told state television.

Khan said his talks with U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright, Secretary of Defence William Cohen and National Security Adviser Samuel Berger would cover Pakistan's dispute with India over Kashmir, the narcotics trade and the fate of F-16 aircraft Pakistan has paid for but not received.
Khan will also meet U.N. Secretary General Kofi Annan.
Khan made clear that Pakistan had not given up hope of getting the F-16s, whose delivery was blocked in 1990 because of suspicions about Islamabad's nuclear programme.

He listed four ways to resolve the issue of the planes, for which Pakistan paid $658 million. The United States could deliver the aircraft, refund the money or sell the planes to a third country and then reimburse Pakistan. The fourth option, he said, was legal action in U.S. courts.
Khan said he favoured the first option, although Congress would have to vote down legislation, known as the Pressler Amendment, which was used to cut off military aid to Pakistan.

The Clinton administration persuaded Congress to ease the sanctions in 1996 when Benazir Bhutto was prime minister, but the F-16s remained blocked. Efforts to sell them to a third country, such as Indonesia, have not succeeded.
Khan will brief his hosts on talks Sharif held with his Indian counterpart Inder Kumar Gujral earlier this month on the sidelines of a regional summit in the Maldives.
The two leaders agreed to keep up a dialogue to ease tension between the South Asian rivals, both seen as threshhold nuclear powers, by setting up working groups to discuss their disputes.
Khan's visit to the United States comes amid a diplomatic row over the detention of a Pakistani employee of the U.S. Drug Enforcement Agency (DEA) working at the U.S. embassy in Islamabad.
The Pakistani Foreign Ministry on Thursday dismissed a U.S. demand for the release of the DEA man, Ayaz Baloch.
A ministry spokesman said Baloch had been arrested on charges of "involvement in drug trafficking and anti-state activities". He was a Pakistani national and would be dealt with under Pakistani law.
The spokesman denied that Baloch's arrest was retaliation for last month's arrest of a Pakistan Air Force officer in New York for allegedly smuggling heroin in a military cargo plane.
